| READ THIS FIRST — WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS AND IS NOT It is not a claim that AI code review is slow. That is a crowded market with no successful independent exit, and IBM Bob already ships a Review workflow. Entering it head-on loses. It is a a bet on the one question no tool and no benchmark in the market asks: whether a change satisfies the requirement it was written against. That gap is structural, not a feature someone forgot. Every number in §3 and §9 is sourced and dated, or explicitly labelled an assumption. The two market figures most likely to be attacked are flagged in place. |
| :---- |

**1   Problem statement**

**AI did not remove the cost of writing code. It moved the cost to checking it — and then it moved on without anyone measuring what that shift left behind.**

**1.1   The constraint has inverted, and it is measurable**

Every tool the market produced answers the question **“is this diff internally correct?”**. The question that now decides whether a change is safe to ship is **“does this change do what the ticket asked for, and does it still respect the rules this system has always obeyed?”** Nothing in the market asks the second question. Not one benchmark scores it. That is not a missing feature — it is a measurement blind spot, and it is the entire basis of this venture.

**1.2   Three compounding failures**

**Failure 1 — supply and demand have inverted**

Code is produced dramatically faster. Shipping it is not faster at all. CircleCI's 2026 telemetry, drawn from 28 million CI/CD workflows across 22,000 organisations, found that the median team's feature-branch throughput rose 15% while its main-branch throughput fell 7%. Main-branch success fell to 70.8%, a five-year low.

This is not a survey. It is instrumented pipeline data, and it is the single most important number in this document: code creation accelerated while delivery decelerated.

**Failure 2 — review is being evicted, not merely delayed**

The market's answer was more automated review. The behavioural data says that answer is not working. 52.8% of bot-reviewed pull requests receive zero human activity after the bot posts its comments, and 84% have no human reviewer besides the author. Between 2025 and 2026, 31% more pull requests began merging with no review at all. Anthropic's own engineering organisation — a frontier lab with unlimited budget — found only 16% of its pull requests received substantive review comments before it built tooling for exactly this.

**Failure 3 — the verification market is structurally blind to intent**

No tool exceeds 63% recall on human-verified issues; the best available misses a third. On pull requests of 1,000 lines or more, aggregate recall falls to 30%. That collapse is not incidental — large-change degradation is precisely the regime where a change's blast radius exceeds the visible diff. It is the invariant problem, measured.

Meanwhile the failure is already surfacing in developer sentiment. In the Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey (n \= 49,000+), 45% named “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite” as their single biggest frustration, 66% reported spending more time fixing almost-right code than before, and only 3% highly trust AI output. DORA's 2025 report records 30% of developers reporting little or no trust in AI-generated code, and names the mechanism the verification tax: time saved in generation is re-spent in audit.

**1.3   The statement**

| PROBLEM STATEMENT The gap between what AI shipped and what was actually verified is unmeasured, unowned and unpriced. No tool tells an engineering organisation whether the code it is reviewing does the thing that was requested — only whether it is internally tidy. Meanwhile review capacity is contracting measurably: reviewers are being replaced by bots whose output humans mostly ignore, and pull requests are merging with no human verification at all. As a result, an organisation cannot see, measure, price or pay down the gap between what its AI-authored code claims to do and what has actually been checked. It discovers the gap the only way it ever does: in production. |
| :---- |

**1.4   Why the obvious product loses**

Before going further, the strongest-seeming version of this idea must be ruled out, because it is the version most teams will build.

| Why “an AI code review bot” is a losing move | Evidence |
| :---- | :---- |
| The category has no successful independent exit. | Graphite acquired by Cursor (Dec 2025). Continue.dev acquired and killed (Jun 2026). Gemini CLI closed in 30 days. Charlie Labs shutting down. |
| Incumbents withdrew even with good metrics. | LlamaPReview shut its paid tier while posting strong numbers, writing that a standalone review bot “is becoming a native IDE feature, not a standalone business.” |
| The platform we are building on already reviews code. | Bob ships a built-in Review workflow with a Findings panel. A submission competing with its own host platform on that axis starts behind. |
| The measurable ceiling is low and falling on large changes. | 63% best-case recall; 30% on 1k+ line pull requests. Every tool degrades on exactly the changes that matter most. |

**So the product must not be a reviewer. It must be a gate that emits evidence — something no native feature will ship, because it requires a corpus and an evidence format rather than an algorithm.**

**2.3   Claim 3 — nobody verifies intent, and here is the proof**

This is the load-bearing claim, so it was verified structurally rather than anecdotally. Martian's Code Review Bench is the only independent evaluator in the category: MIT-licensed, open, 20+ tools evaluated, with both a fixed offline set of 50 pull requests from five major repositories and a live online pipeline sampling fresh pull requests daily.

Its ground truth is constructed two ways, and both are blind to intent:

* **Offline:** human-curated review comments left on historical pull requests — i.e. “what a human noticed in the diff”;  
* **Online:** what the developer actually changed in post-review commits — i.e. “what the bot's comments caused to change in the code.”

| THE CONSEQUENCE — WHY THIS IS A MARKET OPENING, NOT A FEATURE GAP Neither construction asks whether the pull request does what the ticket asked for. A tool that flags ten real bugs in a pull request that implements the wrong requirement scores well on both. A category can be excellent at its stated job, 0% at intent verification, and no leaderboard will ever reveal it. Because there is no score for it, there is no competitive pressure to build it. That is why the capability is available to take, and it is the entire justification for this venture's premise. |
| :---- |

The verification ceiling reinforces the point. No tool exceeds 63% recall; on 1,000+ line pull requests aggregate recall falls to 30%. Large-change degradation is exactly the regime where a change breaks something the diff does not show — a business rule held in someone's head, a rounding convention, an implicit ordering assumption, a decade of production behaviour. IBM's own mainframe modernisation package confronts this directly, and answers it with static analysis for business rules, equivalence tests generated from source behaviour, and runtime tracing. Three expensive mechanisms, available only for COBOL on z/OS.

**The 90%/45% gap is the number that matters commercially: leaders believe they can report on AI's impact, and fewer than half can trace AI activity to specific code changes. That is the traceability deficit this product addresses, stated by people who admit they have it.**

**2.5   What we deliberately do not claim**

Two widely circulated figures are wrong, and using either would be a factual error against the source's own current position.

| Claim you may have seen | Why we are not using it |
| :---- | :---- |
| “Experienced developers were 19% slower with AI” (METR) | Retracted by METR. Their February 2026 update finds late-2025 AI likely accelerated developers on the measured panel. Citing the 19% figure in September 2026 misrepresents the study's own current conclusion. |
| “AI is a thief of time” (attributed to DORA) | This phrase does not appear in any DORA report. DORA's term is the “verification tax”. Using the wrong phrase in front of a DORA-literate audience costs credibility. |

| “Mainframes are dying” | Forrester's 2025 data shows mainframe footprints are growing and the staffing crisis is less severe than projected. Spend is durable and expanding. Any thesis resting on mainframe decline is resting on the wrong premise. |

**3   Solution — the intent attestation gate**

**Not a reviewer. A gate that emits evidence.**

The product reads the requirement where it actually lives, extracts the acceptance criteria, verifies the change against each one under a read-only verifier that cannot modify what it verifies, and emits a per-criterion verdict, a traceability matrix, and a risk-weighted number for everything the gate did not cover. When any criterion is rejected, the merge is blocked.

**3.1   The six stages**

| Stage | What happens | Why it is built this way |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1 · Ingest** | Read the issue, the specification, the PRD, the test matrix and the diff. | IBM Bob 2.0 reads PDF, DOCX, XLSX and images natively. This is a platform capability, not something we build. |
| **2 · Extract criteria** | Pull out atomic acceptance criteria; quality-gate them against ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148\. | Unverifiable criteria are rejected outright rather than silently retained. A criterion that cannot be checked must not create false assurance. |
| **3 · Parse deterministically** | cucumber/gherkin reduces feature files to an AST. | No model in the extraction loop. This is the difference between a credible harness and a demo. |
| **4 · Verify in parallel** | N concurrent read-only workers, one per criterion group, running the probe set. | Bob Shell has no native subagent fan-out — subagents are model-invoked and non-deterministic. We get parallelism by running N independent \`bob run\` processes ourselves. |
| **5 · Adjudicate** | Apply the E0–E6 evidence ladder; issue CERTIFIED / CONDITIONAL / REJECTED. | A single pass/fail is not an audit artefact. The evidence tier behind the verdict is what makes it defensible. |
| **6 · Emit and gate** | Traceability matrix, signed verdict record, review-debt ledger, risk-weighted exposure. Non-zero exit blocks the merge. | The unit of value is a release, not a seat. That is what makes the pricing model work (§7.5). |

**3.2   The probe model**

Per acceptance criterion, five static verification methods, followed by an adversarial pass across seven failure classes. The method is not invented here — it is extracted from the MIT-licensed \`attest\` skill, which already implements this taxonomy.

| Probe | What it establishes | Typical evidence |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **CODE\_SEARCH** | That an implementation artefact exists for this criterion. | Route, handler, component, config reference. |
| **LOGIC\_TRACE** | That business-rule ordering and transformations are correct. | Call chain or condition chain. |
| **STATE\_CHECK** | That state-machine behaviour matches the specification. | Enum, reducer, guard, workflow mapping. |
| **ERROR\_PATH** | That specified failure modes are actually handled. | Error handler, validation, response path. |
| **ABSENCE\_CHECK** | That a required negative is genuinely absent. | Locations searched and the absence of a relevant hit. |

*Adversarial pass: boundary · omission · contradiction · implicit · negative · concurrency. A change that violates an invariant is by definition not visible in the change, so the probes must actively try to break the criterion rather than merely look for its implementation.*

**3.3   Governance by construction**

The most important design decision in the product is a negative one: the verifier runs under a Bob custom mode that grants read, subagent and skill tools and withholds edit and execute entirely. It is structurally incapable of modifying the artefact it attests to, even if instructed to.

| \# .bob/custom\_modes.yaml customModes:   \- slug: attestor     name: Attestor     description: Verifies code against acceptance criteria. Read-only by construction.     roleDefinition: You are an independent verifier. You produce evidence, never changes.     groups:       \- read       \- subagent       \- skill       \- workflow     \# edit and execute are absent, therefore unavailable |
| :---- |

| WHY THIS IS THE DIFFERENTIATOR, NOT A DETAIL The defining failure mode of AI attestation is manufacturing evidence rather than verifying it. In March 2026, former customers of the compliance startup Delve alleged exactly that: fabricated evidence and pre-written auditor conclusions, with 493 of 494 SOC 2 reports found to share near-identical text down to the same grammatical error. The SEC shut down an audit firm in 2024 over fabricated audit documentation behind 1,500+ filings. So this product's differentiator must be independence and verifiability, not throughput. A read-only verifier that runs outside the IDE, on a different model, and cannot touch the artefact is a structural answer. A prompt that says “be honest” is not. If an auditor or regulator has been burned by Delve, this is the first question they will ask — the answer has to be architecture, not policy. |
| :---- |

**3.4   What the gate emits**

| Artefact | Contents | Consumer |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Per-criterion verdict record | CERTIFIED / CONDITIONAL / REJECTED, the evidence tier, the probe results, and the exact locations examined. | The reviewer deciding whether to trust the change. |
| Traceability matrix | Acceptance criterion → implementing code → the test that proves it. Bidirectional. | The auditor. This is the artefact that answers “show me the coverage”. |
| Review-debt ledger | What is NOT covered: changes merged with no human reviewer, no automated review, or no applicable criteria. Weighted by realised defect rate. | VP Engineering as a release-velocity instrument; the risk function as an exposure number. |
| Risk-weighted exposure | A single number per repository and per business capability, with a decay curve over time. | The quarterly audit committee conversation. |
| Signed evidence record | Tamper-evident, hash-chained, exportable. | Second line of defence and internal audit. |

**3.5   The measurable claim — and why it is defensible**

A product that cannot be measured is a product that cannot be sold, funded or trusted. This one produces a number nobody else in the market can produce, because the number comes from a measurement blind spot rather than from competing on a leaderboard.

| THE PUBLISHABLE METRIC FALSE CERTIFIED RATE  \=  P( verdict \= CERTIFIED  |  a specification violation is actually present ) Measured by taking real acceptance criteria, injecting a known defect operator into each, and recording how often the gate still certifies. Reported per operator class, because a single aggregate number hides the finding. |
| :---- |

Seven operator classes, taken from the mutation-testing literature's own “specification mutation” category — the category in which faults are seeded into specifications rather than source code:

| Operator class | Mutation applied to a real criterion |
| :---- | :---- |
| Boundary drop | remove the upper or lower bound from a stated range |
| Comparison inversion | flip “older than 30 days” to “30 days or newer” |
| Threshold weakening | change a numeric limit from 30 days to 90 |
| Error-path deletion | remove the requirement to reject invalid input |
| Normative demotion | demote MUST to SHOULD |
| Negative-constraint removal | delete “and no state change” |
| Untestability | replace a checkable criterion with a vague one |

Free corroborating \! exists on the code side. A Stryker Mutator “Survived” mutant is a machine-located real defect with an exact file and line: behaviour that is live in the code and undetected by the test suite. That gives an independent, reproducible fault list without hand-seeding anything.

| WHY THE OSS SWARM IS NOT ALREADY DONE THIS The primitives are genuinely free and MIT-licensed — the \`attest\` skill, Stryker, cucumber/gherkin, and Martian's benchmark harness. Four of the six projects commonly cited in this space, however, are closed-source SaaS with zero public repositories, and one promising repository is private. The defensible asset is not the algorithm. It is a vertical corpus of regulator-grade acceptance criteria plus an evidence format an auditor accepts — neither of which can be scraped, and both of which compound. |
| :---- |

**5   Step-by-step operating procedure**

Concrete operating procedure for the prototype, and the design it implies. Command syntax has been verified against the shipped IBM Bob 2.0 binary (v2.0.5), not only against documentation — several documented details are wrong.

**5.1   Stage 0 — environment**

**1\.	Account.** Confirm the hackathon-provisioned account is active (“ibm-hackathon-xxxx”, Enterprise plan, us-east). Using a personal account burns personal Bobcoins and disqualifies the evidence.

**2\.	Versions.** Bob IDE must be v2.0.2 or later. Versions 1.0.3 and 2.0.0 stop working on 30 September 2026\.

**3\.	Runtime.** Node.js 22 or later (the docs say 24; the binary's engine field says \>=22, and 22 works).

| curl \-fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | bash bob \--version          \# expect 2.0.5 or later export BOB\_API\_KEY="..."   \# API key with Scope \= Inference; this is the ONLY correct name |
| :---- |

| VERIFIED TRAPS — these will cost you hours if you trust the docs BOBSHELL\_API\_KEY is a legacy alias. Setting both to different values throws. Use BOB\_API\_KEY. The flag is \--mode, not \--chat-mode. There is no \--sandbox flag. \--yolo is deprecated and ignored. Headless runs already auto-approve every tool — which means bob run in CI is unsandboxed. Constrain it with \--disable-tool-groups and \--max-cost. Token counts are documented in the \--format json schema but are gated behind a hardcoded-false condition in the shipped binary. They will never appear. Use stats.session\_costs instead. status: "success" is hardcoded in the non-stream path. Branch on the process exit code, not the JSON status. |
| :---- |

**5.2   Stage 1 — ingest the requirement**

**1\.**	Pull the issue body and its acceptance-criteria section. Filter for criteria that are actually filled: at least two completed checklist items. Unfilled template scaffolding must be rejected, or the dataset is mostly noise.

**2\.**	Retrieve the diff and its commit ancestry. If a specification document exists, hand the path to Bob directly — PDF, DOCX and XLSX are read natively, so no extraction step is needed.

| \# one deterministic parse, no model in the loop gh issue view 2298 \--repo TYPO3BestPractices/tea \--json body,title \> issue.json gh pr diff \<PR\> \--repo TYPO3BestPractices/tea \> change.diff \# Bob reads the document natively \-- no copy-paste, no separate extraction step bob run \--format json \--max-cost 3 "Extract every acceptance criterion from @spec.pdf as a numbered list. Reject any criterion that is not atomic and testable." |
| :---- |

**5.3   Stage 2 — quality-gate the criteria**

**1\.**	Apply the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 characteristics that can be checked mechanically: atomicity, presence of a testability construct, and absence of banned vague terms such as “etc.”, “as needed”, “user-friendly”, “appropriate”, “fast”.

**2\.**	Be honest about what cannot be checked. Unambiguity, completeness and feasibility are semantic. No regex linter can certify them — two independent open-source sources make the same admission. Those require the adversarial pass and a human gate, not a keyword check.

**3\.**	Emit the criteria set with any rejects recorded explicitly, so a rejected criterion is visible rather than absent.

**5.4   Stage 3 — fan out the verification fleet**

This is the stage the hackathon rubric rewards explicitly — parallel tasks and subagents — and the stage where Bob's real behaviour must be worked around rather than assumed.

| \# .bob/custom\_modes.yaml \-- the read-only constraint, enforced by the harness customModes:   \- slug: attestor     name: Attestor     description: Verifies code against acceptance criteria. Read-only.     roleDefinition: You are an independent verifier. You produce evidence, never changes.     whenToUse: Use when checking whether a change satisfies a stated requirement.     groups: \[read, subagent, skill, workflow\] \# run N workers concurrently; N is bounded by the Bobcoin budget, not by rate limits for grp in 1 2 3 4; do   bob run \--mode attestor \--format stream-json \\          \--max-cost 4 \--max-turns 40 \--trust \\          "Verify criteria group \$grp against the change. Emit one verdict per           criterion as JSON: {id, verdict, evidence\_tier, probes, locations}." & done; wait |
| :---- |

| WHY WE RUN N PROCESSES INSTEAD OF RELYING ON SUBAGENTS Bob's subagent tool is model-invoked. The documentation is explicit that Bob spawns a subagent only when a task is genuinely self-contained, and there is no CLI flag, syntax or API to force fan-out. You cannot make it deterministic; you can only ask for it in the prompt. Parallelism therefore comes from launching N independent bob run processes and aggregating their JSON. This is also what the hackathon is rewarding when it asks for “parallel tasks and subagents” — and it is deterministic, which matters for a benchmark. Bob documents no rate or concurrency limits. Parallel invocations are not blocked client-side. The real constraint is Bobcoins, and parallel jobs multiply spend — so \--max-cost per worker is not optional, it is the budget. |
| :---- |

**5.5   Stage 4 — adjudicate and emit**

**1\.**	Apply the evidence ladder. Criteria whose security or data impact implies a floor of E4 demand property, metamorphic, mutation, fuzz or differential evidence — automated tests alone do not clear them. Write the tier into the verdict record.

**2\.**	Classify each criterion CERTIFIED, CONDITIONAL or REJECTED.

**3\.**	Assemble the traceability matrix: criterion → implementing code → proving test, bidirectionally, so both “is this criterion covered?” and “why does this code exist?” are answerable.

**4\.**	Compute the review-debt ledger and the risk-weighted exposure number for everything outside the gate's coverage.

| \# gate behaviour: non-zero exit blocks the merge if any verdict \== REJECTED and verdict.evidence\_tier \< required\_tier:     print(json.dumps(traceability\_matrix, indent=2))   \# to the PR     gh pr comment \$PR \--body-file matrix.md     sys.exit(1)          \# blocks merge sys.exit(0)              \# all criteria cleared |
| :---- |

**5.6   Stage 5 — the evaluation harness**

This is what turns a prototype into a publishable result, and it is the part that earns the venture claim.

**1\.**	Harvest real criteria from a permissively-licensed public repository where issues carry genuine acceptance criteria and pull requests close them.

**2\.**	For each criterion, run every operator class and record whether the gate still emits CERTIFIED. That is a false-certified event.

**3\.**	Score both our gate and at least one conventional review tool on the same mutated specifications, so the comparison is like-for-like.

**4\.**	Report per operator class, publish the harness, and publish the limitations alongside the numbers.

| Dataset | Licence | Why | Size |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **TYPO3BestPractices/tea** | GPL-2.0 | 10 MB, AC-structured epic/story/task issues, 345 issues closed by a linked PR. Clones and indexes in about an hour. | 10 MB |
| **SAP-cloud-infrastructure/elektra** | Apache-2.0 | Best licence hygiene; proves the result is not overfit to one repository. | 84 MB |
| **IntersectMBO/cardano-addresses** | Apache-2.0 | Second Apache-2.0 confirmation set. | 91 MB |

| THE DATA-CLEANING TRAP — THIS WILL SILENTLY POISON THE RESULTS Many issues containing the heading “Acceptance criteria” contain the unfilled template — for example “Add AC's here..” and “Regression testing (if applicable)”. Filter for at least two *filled* checklist items, not for the heading. Get this wrong and the dataset is mostly template noise, which is exactly what a sceptical reviewer will assume. |
| :---- |

**6   Build plan, team allocation and budget**

**6.1   Five people, five critical paths**

The 40-Bobcoin budget is a team pool, not a per-member allowance, and every member must separately produce qualifying Bob task sessions for the mandatory bob\_sessions/ evidence. The allocation below keeps every member on a real code path — no one is given a supporting role that produces no Bob evidence.

| Member | Critical path | Produces | Bobcoins |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | ----: |
| A | Dataset & harness | Extraction of real (issue, criteria, PR) triples; the unfilled-template filter; operator injection; the scoring harness. | **6** |
| B | Verifier core | The attestor custom mode, the probe set, the per-criterion verdict schema, and the evidence ladder. | **12** |
| C | Pipeline & gate | Orchestration of the parallel fleet, cost metering from session\_costs, exit-code gating, the traceability matrix. | **9** |
| D | Artefacts & demo | The evidence artefacts, the review-debt ledger, the exposure number, the HTML one-pager, and the demo narrative. | **7** |
| E | Estate & integration | The simulated COBOL/JCL estate, the business-rule set, and the watsonx Orchestrate MCP tool. | **6** |

*Reserve 4 Bobcoins unallocated as contingency. Once usage reaches 100% no further Bobcoins are provided, and work can continue — but the AI features stop, which means the demo cannot be regenerated.*

**6.2   Sequenced against the clock**

| Window | Objective | Done when |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Hour 0–1 | Environment, accounts, versions, repository, commit early. | Repo exists and is public. \`bob run\` returns valid JSON once. |
| Hour 1–3 | **MANDATORY ARTEFIRST SECURED.** Commit the first bob\_sessions/ screenshots and a working README before anything else. | bob\_sessions/ is in the repo with per-member PNGs. This is the only non-negotiable requirement. |
| Hour 3–7 | Dataset extraction running in parallel with the verifier core. | ≥ 200 real criteria with ≥ 2 filled items, linked to closing PRs. |
| Hour 7–13 | The attestor mode and the probe set working end to end on one criterion. | One criterion produces a real per-criterion verdict with evidence tier. |
| Hour 13–18 | Parallel fleet, cost metering, merge gating. | N workers run concurrently within budget; a REJECTED verdict blocks a merge. |
| Hour 18–24 | The evaluation harness on mutated specifications. | False-certified rate computed per operator class, with a conventional comparison. |
| Hour 24–30 | Artefacts, the simulated estate, the demo narrative. | Traceability matrix, ledger, exposure number and one-pager all present. |
| Final 2h | Freeze. Regenerate every screenshot. Verify the repository submission requirements end to end. | Nothing is being changed that has not been screenshotted. |

**6.3   The submission requirements, precisely**

| Requirement | Detail |
| :---- | :---- |
| Bob IDE as a core component | The only hard eligibility gate. “Your solution must showcase IBM Bob IDE as a core component.” Bob Shell and skills are the same agent, so a Bob Shell-driven pipeline satisfies this — but the evidence screenshots must come from the IDE. |
| bob\_sessions/ folder | At the repository root. PNG format where possible. Filename pattern “team\_taskNN\_short-description\_summary.png”. |
| Per participant | Each participant must upload their own Bob task-session summaries. Screenshot path: Bob IDE → Tasks → select task (or “All” across workspaces) → select the task header → capture the consumption summary. |
| Data compliance | No confidential data, no client data, no personal information, no social-media data. Public data is permitted where terms allow commercial use — keep the list of source websites in the repository. |

| A NOTE ON TEAM SIZE Five members is workable but carries a real cost: five separate sets of qualifying Bob task sessions are mandatory, per person. That is more Bob work, not less, and Bobcoins are a shared pool. The mitigation is the allocation in §6.1 — every member owns a code path that generates sessions naturally. If the team can be reduced to three without losing a path, the budget per person roughly doubles. |
| :---- |

**7   Venture research**

**7.1   The category we are deliberately not entering**

The AI code review category is closed and consolidating. This is the single most important commercial finding in this document, and it is the reason the product is shaped as a gate rather than a reviewer.

| Outcome | Company | Detail |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Acquired | Graphite | Acquired by Cursor, December 2025\. |
| Acquired and killed | Continue.dev | Acquired June 2026, then shut down. |
| Closed in 30 days | Gemini CLI | Rapid deprecation. |
| Wound down | Charlie Labs, Flowise | Shutdown following acquisition. |
| **Exited voluntarily, with good metrics** | LlamaPReview | Shut its paid tier while posting strong numbers, writing that a standalone review bot “is becoming a native IDE feature, not a standalone business.” |

Capital is real but concentrated at the top of a closed category: CodeRabbit at a \$1.5B valuation and \$231M raised, Qodo at \$120M. Competing there is not a bet worth making.

**7.2   Where the defensible position actually is**

Five candidate gaps were tested adversarially. They do not survive scrutiny equally.

| Candidate gap | Verdict | Reasoning |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Review in the context of system history and architecture | **NOT A GAP** | Being commoditised in real time. Augment shipped its context index as a free MCP server in February 2026\. Qodo markets full-repository signals including codebase history and prior PR decisions. The index is the durable primitive and it is being given away. |
| Verify the change satisfies the original requirement | **OPEN** | A measurement blind spot, not a feature gap — so no competitive pressure to close it and no leaderboard credit for closing it. See §2.3. |
| Detect silent invariant or contract breakage | **OPEN AND EXPENSIVE** | Real, and mapped to a budget engineering does not own. The buyer is risk and audit, not the VP Engineering. That mismatch is precisely why it is defensible. |
| Attribute risky code to a specific agent or prompt | **CAPABILITY IS A COMMODITY** | prompt-bom, ForgeProof, licit and squash are free and open, already covering Ed25519 signing, SPDX 3.0, CycloneDX 1.7 ML-BOM and in-toto attestations. Entering a spec race we would lose. The scarce asset is the correlation model, which needs 6–12 months of volume. |
| Quantify review debt — the unreviewed backlog | **REAL AND UNOWNED** | Every vendor sells reviews performed. Nobody sells the reviews not done, risk-weighted, with a decay curve. But it is a negative metric with no budget line of its own — so it is an input to a wedge, not a wedge on its own. |

| THE SYNTHESIS Sell the gate and the evidence, never the review. The gate is what cannot be bundled into an IDE, because it needs a corpus and an evidence format rather than an algorithm. The review-debt ledger is how we sell it — it is the number that makes the gap urgent. And the attribution correlation model is the data moat we accumulate while the gate runs. |
| :---- |

**7.3   Why this is defensible**

| Moat element | Why it holds | Time to build |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Vertical corpus of regulator-grade acceptance criteria | Cannot be scraped. A few thousand real criteria for one domain, mapped to the tests that prove them, is what an auditor actually asks for — and it is not derivable from public data. | 6–12 months, and it is the real company |
| An auditor-acceptable evidence format | Compounds with the corpus and is not bought. The format is the product as far as internal audit is concerned. | 3–6 months |
| Model and vendor independence | The verifier runs outside the IDE, on a different model, read-only. That is what makes it credible evidence rather than a vendor's own homework. | Immediate, by construction |
| The review-debt dataset | Improves with every attested release and cannot be reconstructed from public data. A data moat, not a technology moat — and it only pays after volume. | Pays from month 6–12 |
| IBM's structural conflict of interest | IBM cannot credibly grade code produced by Bob, and cannot endorse a rival's validator. It can list an independent one in its own catalog. This is an opening, not a moat — a 12–24 month window at most. | Window, not asset |

**7.4   Pricing — and why per-seat is already dead**

The category's two largest players abandoned seat pricing within twelve months. Any model that prices per developer inherits a problem that has already been solved by the incumbents.

| Product | Model | Change |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Cursor Bugbot | \$1.00–\$1.50 per run | Abandoned \$40 per seat. |
| Greptile | \$1 per review | Added usage pricing. |
| GitHub Copilot | AI credits | Moved away from seat bundles. |
| IBM Bob | Bobcoins (1 \= \$0.50) | Enterprise packs of 1,000 coins for \$500. |
| Intercom Fin | \$0.99 per confirmed resolution | The outcome-pricing precedent. |

| OUR PRICING — PER ATTESTED RELEASE Two components: a platform fee of roughly \$85K ACV for the gate, the evidence format and the portal; plus a variable tier of about \$100 per attested application per year at an assumed 30% attach rate across roughly 1,500 applications in year one. Why this works: the unit is a *release* — discrete, countable and forecastable. It sidesteps both the seat-pricing collapse and the CIO's distrust of open-ended variance-based outcome pricing, because “a release” is not a vague outcome. It is the cleanest available fit to selling the work rather than the tool, without taking unbounded outcome risk. It also does not scale with headcount, which is the point. A tool priced per seat is punished the moment the seat count is scrutinised — and this buyer is not a developer. |
| :---- |

**7.5   Go-to-market**

| Phase | Motion | Target |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Beachhead | Design partners inside IBM Z accounts specifically — where incumbent review tools are weakest, the code is highest-stakes, and the buyer has an existing budget line. | 3–5 design partners. Conversations, not revenue. |
| Land | Ship the gate inside one modernisation programme. The reference logo matters more than the ACV. | 1 paying account with a public case study. |
| Channel | Submit an MCP tool to watsonx Orchestrate Agent Connect — a live, populated catalog already carrying third-party partner agents and MCP servers, supporting both MCP and A2A. | Catalog listing, IBM-led go-to-market. |
| Expand | Generalise the corpus from mainframe to adjacent regulated portfolios, then to the broader evidence-and-assurance pool. | The \$3.2–5.0B pool in §9.4. |

*The channel argument in one sentence, from an investor rather than from IBM: organisations “will increasingly need independent governance layers that can validate software regardless of which model produced it.” IBM cannot build that credibly, because it would be grading its own homework. It can list it.*

**7.6   The buyer is not the developer**

This is the commercial point most likely to be missed. The user of an AI review tool is a developer, and developers do not buy \$85K software. The buyer is engineering leadership plus the audit and compliance function — and the compliance function has a budget, a mandatory-spend character, and no self-serve option. That is how a developer tool escapes the trap of dying at a \$30K ACV with weak net retention.

| Persona | What they are measured on | The line that lands |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| VP Engineering | Release velocity, change failure rate, developer time, review-debt exposure. | “41% of agent-authored changes touching the payments ledger merged with no human review. Here is the burn-down.” |
| Head of Modernisation | Programme schedule, equivalence assurance, audit findings. | “Every attested application ships with a criterion-level equivalence record instead of a manual documentation exercise.” |
| Compliance / Audit / Risk | Findings, attestability, evidence integrity, regulatory exposure. | “Your auditor can verify the evidence, not trust the platform.” |
| CISO | Data residency, sovereignty, model independence, evidence integrity. | “Runs in your enclave, on your model, and cannot modify what it verifies.” |

**7.7   Risks, stated plainly**

A document that lists no weaknesses invites the reader to assume none were found. These are the real ones.

| Risk | Severity | Assessment and mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| A major incumbent ships acceptance-criteria verification as a feature | **HIGH** | LinearB already markets “AI Code Reviews — catch security risks, bugs, and spec mismatches.” Momentic's knowledge base already arbitrates real-bug versus intended-change. CodeRabbit's triage surface is one release away. Mitigation: none of these ships criterion-level evidence; the corpus is the moat, and it takes longer than a sprint. |
| IBM bundles an equivalent into a Premium Package at zero price | **HIGH** | Bob Premium Package for Z went GA on 9 July 2026 and already owns COBOL business-rule extraction and equivalence testing. It could plausibly extend to attestation. Mitigation: be genuinely model-agnostic and genuinely outside the Bob IDE, so we are more useful to IBM as a catalog partner than as a rival. |
| Evidence manufacturing — the Delve failure mode | **HIGH** | Our category's defining scandal is producing evidence rather than verifying it. Mitigation: read-only verifier, external to the IDE, model-independent, signed chain. Independence is the product, not a feature of it. |
| The open-source swarm operationalises this first | **MEDIUM** | The primitives are free and MIT-licensed, and several solo projects are working the same idea. Mitigation: none has a regulated corpus or an accepted evidence format, and those are the two things that compound. |
| Compliance framing is legally overreaching | **MEDIUM** | EU AI Act Article 12 binds only high-risk AI systems, and minimum log content is mandated only for remote biometric identification. Any pitch claiming the Act requires AI-code traceability for ordinary software is wrong and will be caught. DORA is the stronger and safer forcing function for a bank buyer: already in force, directly applicable, with named articles on ICT third-party risk. |
| Certification and procurement friction | **MEDIUM** | Cloud-only incumbents are structurally disqualified for air-gapped and sovereign buyers, but that is only an advantage if we actually ship an air-gapped build. No reliable sales-cycle data exists for this category; do not plan against a number nobody can source. |
| Market size — see §9.4 | **HIGH** | The beachhead alone does not support a venture-scale outcome. This is stated plainly rather than engineered away. |

**8   Target market**

**8.1   Ideal customer profile**

| Dimension | Beachhead | Expansion |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Estate | IBM Z / z/OS, COBOL and RPG workloads | Mixed estates undergoing AI-assisted modernisation |
| Sector | Banking and insurance | Government, healthcare, utilities |
| Size | \> 1,000 employees (93.75% of IBM Z customers already qualify) | Same, plus mid-market financial services |
| Geography | US, UK, Germany | EU-wide |
| Trigger | An active modernisation or AI-adoption programme with an audit deadline attached | A production incident traced to unverified AI output |
| Budget owner | Modernisation programme lead, second-line risk | CISO and internal audit |

**8.2   Why this segment, and not a more obvious one**

* **Density.** 71% of the Fortune 500 run mainframes, and more than 90% of financial-services organisations do. 44 of the top 50 banks and all of the top 10 insurers.  
* **Durability.** 88% of mainframe users expect continued reliance for five years or more, and 54% plan to expand their mainframe use cases. Only 15% plan to reduce reliance. The spend is durable — and the reframe is that money going into staying and extending, not exiting.  
* **Weakness of alternatives.** The incumbent review tools are weakest here. The code is COBOL and PL/I, the business rules are undocumented, and the blast radius of a wrong change is a regulated ledger.  
* **Budget line.** IBM's own Premium Package for Z already extracts business rules and generates equivalence tests from source behaviour. The category exists, is named, and is budgeted — we are entering a spending line, not creating one.

**8.3   Expansion path**

| Stage | What changes | Why it is reachable |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 · IBM Z regulated | Vertical corpus: one domain, one estate type. | The corpus is domain-specific, so this is where it must start anyway. |
| 2 · Adjacent regulated estates | Second corpus, second domain. | Same engine, same evidence format. Marginal cost is the corpus. |
| 3 · Government and public sector | Same proof obligations, different buyer. | Named as a target vertical of the published category definition. |
| 4 · Horizontal evidence and assurance | The product becomes a release gate for any regulated codebase. | This is the \$3.2–5.0B pool. See §9.4. |

**8.4   The regulatory clock**

| Instrument | Status | What it actually requires — and does not |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **EU AI Act**Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 | In force 1 Aug 2024\. Generally applicable 2 Aug 2026\. High-risk under Annex III from 2 Dec 2027; Annex I from 2 Aug 2028\. The AI Omnibus entered into force 27 July 2026, moving the high-risk dates later but fixing them in law. | Annex IV ¶2(g) requires dated and signed test logs for high-risk systems. Penalties reach €15M or 3% of turnover. BUT Article 12 binds only high-risk AI systems, and its minimum log content is mandated only for remote biometric identification. It does not make AI-code traceability mandatory for ordinary enterprise software. Harmonised standards are not due before Q4 2026\. |
| **DORA**Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 | Directly applicable since 17 January 2025\. No national transposition. Supervisory relationship is already live. | Articles 28–30 on ICT third-party risk. This is the stronger forcing function for a bank buyer, because it is a live supervisory relationship rather than a future compliance project. |
| **NIS2**Directive (EU) 2022/2555 | Transposition deadline was 17 October 2024; applies from 18 October 2024\. Still fragmenting across member states. | Do not build a revenue model on NIS2 enforcement dates. It is two years past deadline and still incomplete. |
| **Cyber Resilience Act**Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 | In force 10 December 2024\. Main obligations apply 11 December 2027\. | The sleeper — the only EU regulation making software vulnerability handling mandatory on a manufacturer basis. But incumbent tooling already ships CRA compliance. |

| THE HONEST COMPLIANCE POSITION Regulation is a forcing function, not our product. The defensible claim is that attestation is how an organisation demonstrates control — and the enforcement surface is narrower than the sales narrative usually assumes. Any competent customer will catch an overreach, and a compliance buyer is the one buyer whose scepticism is fatal to the deal. State the narrow claim. |
| :---- |

**9   TAM / SAM / SOM model**

Account-based, not developer-based. The arithmetic is shown so it can be attacked line by line, and every input is labelled sourced or assumed.

![][image3]

*Figure 3 — TAM / SAM / SOM with the account funnel. Every assumption is labelled; the weakest is marked in red.*

**9.1   Why account-based**

Developer-population sizing was rejected outright. SlashData puts 7.5M developers at large enterprises, but effectively none of them work on IBM Z, and this product prices per account and per portfolio rather than per seat. Applying a per-seat price to the enterprise developer population would overstate this market by at least an order of magnitude.

**9.2   The funnel, step by step**

| Step | Calculation | Low | Base | High | Label |
| :---- | :---- | ----: | ----: | ----: | :---- |
| Global IBM Z / z/OS enterprises | vendor counts | 2,844 | **6,276** | 15,957 | SOURCED — but vendors disagree 5.6× |
| × geography (US 44% \+ UK 11% \+ DE 9%) | × 0.64 | 1,820 | **4,017** | 10,212 | SOURCED — and a floor, since the 21% RoW bucket is excluded |
| × \> 1,000 employees | × 0.9375 | 1,706 | **3,766** | 9,574 | SOURCED — 93.75% already qualify, so this filter does little work |
| × banking \+ insurance | × 0.30 | 427 | **1,130** | 3,351 | **ASSUMPTION — the weakest input** |
| **\= SAM accounts** |  | 427 | **1,130** | 3,351 |  |
| × platform ACV \$85K | × 85,000 | \$21.4M | **\$96.1M** | \$502.7M | ASSUMPTION — benchmarked to Vanta Enterprise top-end |
| \+ variable tier | 30% × 1,500 apps × \$100 | \$3.2M | **\$50.9M** | \$804.0M | ASSUMPTION — all three inputs unsourced |
| **\= SAM revenue** |  | \$24.6M | **\$147M** | \$1,306.7M | **Do not plan against the high case** |

TAM drops the geography and vertical gates and adds government at 40%: 5,884 accounts, approximately \$306M annually — 2.08× SAM, consistent with the wider gates.

**9.3   SOM — and the honest ceiling**

The binding constraint is distribution, not market size. The comparable that sets the ceiling is Vanta: about eight years, \$300M ARR, 16,000 customers and over \$500M raised to sell compliance automation to enterprises.

| THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MORE THAN ANY TAM Vanta's \$300M ARR is 2.0× this product's entire base-case SAM. The most successful compliance-automation company ever built could not exceed the size of this product's entire beachhead. That is not a criticism of the market — it is a statement about the beachhead. IBM Z is a credibility mechanism and an entry point, not the size of the business. |
| :---- |

**9.4   The real market, and why we say so plainly**

The published category definitions are small, and the small number is the wrong one to lead with. Attestation revenue does not land in “AI governance platforms”; it lands in the evidence-and-assurance layer of GRC and application security.

| Category | 2026 size | Source | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| AI governance platforms | \$492M | Gartner | Smallest credible estimate of the smallest relevant category. Do not lead with it. |
| AI Code Review & SDLC Governance | \~\$1.1B | YH Research / MarketPublishers, 15.5% CAGR | A named category with “release compliance gating” as an explicit sub-segment and financial IT as a named vertical. Three houses invented it independently. |
| GRC software — evidence slice (10–20%) | \$0.5–1.8B | derived from Verdantix | Where audit and attestation budgets actually sit. |
| AppSec — evidence slice (10–15%) | \$1.1–1.65B | derived from Juniper \$11B | Overlaps heavily with the GRC slice. |
| **Total addressable** | **\$3.2–5.0B** |  | At 2–4% share: \$64M–\$202M serviceable at maturity. |

| THE STRATEGIC HONESTY OF THIS DOCUMENT The beachhead SAM is roughly \$147M. The category-expansion pool is \$3.2–5.0B. The venture-scale outcome lives in the second number, and the first number is how we earn the right to reach it. A document that presented \$147M as the opportunity would be flattering and wrong. A document that presented only the \$5B would be unfalsifiable. Both are given, with the arithmetic visible. |

| Weakness | Severity | How it was handled |

| Enterprise-count denominator is unknown. Technographic vendors report 2,844 / 6,276 / 15,957 — a 5.6× spread. IBM does not disclose customer counts. | **HIGH** | The whole model is run as a range. Cross-checked against 71% of the Fortune 500 \= 355 US companies, which agrees in order of magnitude. |
| Banking and insurance share of 30% is a pure assumption. | **HIGH** | Labelled as the weakest input in the model and in the figure. No published figure exists. |
| COBOL-in-production volume cannot be pinned down. | MEDIUM | Credible range is 220B (2017) to 850B (2022), a 3.5× spread. The upper bound is vendor-commissioned. Used only directionally, never as a sizing input. |
| No reliable sales-cycle data for regulated dev tooling. | MEDIUM | Stated as a gap. No revenue model is built on an unsourced cycle. |

**10   Future plans**

**10.1    The next 48 hours**

| Priority | Deliverable | Success criterion |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| P0 | bob\_sessions/ evidence secured in the repository within the first three hours. | Committed before anything else is at risk of being broken. |
| P0 | One criterion verified end to end with a real evidence tier. | Not a mock. A real verdict from the read-only mode. |
| P1 | Parallel fleet running within budget. | N concurrent workers, metered from session\_costs. |
| P1 | False-certified rate computed per operator class. | The publishable number, with limitations stated. |
| P2 | Merge gate blocks on a REJECTED verdict. | Demonstrated on a real pull request. |
| P2 | Simulated COBOL/JCL estate with a business-rule set. | The story judges will remember. |

**10.2    Months 0–6 — from prototype to product**

**1\.**	Replace the heuristic criterion extraction with a governed process and an explicit rejection record. Every rejected criterion must be visible.

**2\.**	Add runtime verification — generate and run the test — to close the loop from static conformance to behavioural proof. Static evidence alone will not satisfy an auditor.

**3\.**	Build the review-debt ledger properly, on CODEOWNERS-based required-reviewer coverage. This is the only normative definition available: DORA's four-keys model contains no review-coverage metric, and that absence is the gap we fill.

**4\.**	Ship the signed, hash-chained, exportable evidence record and publish the control mapping. Content, not product, and it is the door-opener for a security review.

**5\.**	Land three to five design partners inside IBM Z accounts specifically.

**6\.**	Submit an MCP tool to watsonx Orchestrate Agent Connect.

**10.3    Months 6–12 — the moat**

**1\.**	Assemble the first vertical corpus: several thousand regulator-grade acceptance criteria for one domain, mapped to the tests that prove them. This is the actual company. It is not scrapeable and it is what an auditor asks for.

**2\.**	Begin accumulating the agent-risk correlation model: which agent, at which prompt version, on which task class, correlates with defect escape and rollback in this codebase under this team's workflow. Sell the correlation, never the ledger — provenance infrastructure is free and open, and that is a spec race we would lose.

**3\.**	Start SOC 2 Type II. It is table stakes rather than a differentiator — the incumbents already have it — but it cannot be started late.

**4\.**	Publish the first real risk findings and the benchmark, openly. Being the reference measurement is worth more than any feature.

**10.4    Months 12–24 — expansion**

**1\.**	Second vertical corpus in an adjacent regulated domain. Same engine, marginal cost is the corpus alone.

**2\.**	One certification path: FedRAMP Moderate, a DORA operational-resilience pack, or ISO/IEC 42001\. The last is fastest and increasingly the AI-specific one.

**3\.**	Ship the air-gapped and on-premises build. The incumbents' cloud-only architecture is a decision they cannot cheaply reverse, and it is what disqualifies them for sovereign buyers.

**4\.**	Generalise to a horizontal release gate for any regulated codebase — the \$3.2–5.0B pool.

**10.5    What would make us stop**

A strategy that cannot be falsified is not a strategy. Three findings would mean this is the wrong bet, and each is observable within roughly two quarters.

| Falsifier | How we would detect it | Then what |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| A major incumbent ships criterion-level evidence with an auditor-accepted format. | Tracking CodeRabbit, Qodo, LinearB and Momentic release notes and changelogs monthly. | The moat was the corpus and someone built it faster. Exit or pivot to the vertical. |
| IBM ships attestation inside a Premium Package at no incremental price. | Tracking Bob Premium Package release notes; Z and i packages are versioned publicly. | The independent-validator opening closes. Exit. |
| Design partners will not pay for the evidence. | If five design-partner conversations produce zero paid conversions by month nine. | The compliance budget was not the buyer we thought. Re-test the ICP before spending on the corpus. |

**10.6    The one-sentence version**

| Every AI review tool on earth asks “is this diff tidy?”  We ask “does this code do what the ticket said?” — and we publish the rate at which that question goes unanswered today, per defect class, in a form anyone can reproduce. |

**A.4   Reusable open source**

| Component | What we take from it | Licence |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **simota/agent-skills → attest** | The probe taxonomy (CODE\_SEARCH, LOGIC\_TRACE, STATE\_CHECK, ERROR\_PATH, ABSENCE\_CHECK), CERTIFIED/CONDITIONAL/REJECTED, the six adversarial categories, the E0–E6 evidence ladder, the ISO 29148 gate. | MIT |
| **withmartian/code-review-benchmark** | Harness methodology: F-beta scoring, category profiles, matched-excluded handling, greedy assignment. Steps 2–5 reusable directly. | MIT |
| **stryker-mutator** | Survived mutants as machine-located known faults with exact file:line. Verified working during research. | Apache-2.0 |
| **cucumber/gherkin** | Deterministic feature-file parsing to an AST — no model in the extraction loop. | MIT |
| **bmw-software-engineering/trlc, lobster** | The only machine-checkable requirements formalism in existence. Read the method; do not link — GPL/AGPL. | GPL-3.0 / AGPL-3.0 |

| WHAT IS NOT ACTUALLY OPEN SOURCE Four projects commonly cited in this space have no public code: godriftless.ai (org has zero public repos), spectrace.io (org has zero public repos), vaspera-pm (installable, but the repository named in package.json returns 404), and openagile.ai (no organisation exists). Do not plan around building on them. |

**A.5   Gaps — what could not be verified**

* Any quantified enterprise bus-factor or developer onboarding-time figure.  
* A reliable average sales-cycle length for AI code review in regulated industries.  
* A figure for SCA alerts per pull request, or the percentage that are false positives.  
* IBM's absolute IBM Z revenue — IBM discloses only percentage change, so it cannot be derived.  
* FedRAMP RFC-0024 and the current US federal software-bill-of-materials position.  
* Whether any Menlo Ventures 2026 enterprise-AI report exists; the latest located is December 2025, so agent-adoption figures remain genuinely contested (19% to 67% depending on the definition of “deployed”).

**B   Open decisions and assumptions register**

Three questions raised during framing were not answered before this document was produced. Rather than bury the guesses, they are recorded here as explicit assumptions, together with what changes if each is wrong.

| \# | Decision | Assumption used here | If it is wrong |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Q4 | Real OSS dataset vs purpose-built codebase | **60/40 split.** Extraction from TYPO3BestPractices/tea and two Apache-2.0 repositories for the defensible spec-mutation numbers; one purpose-built COBOL/JCL estate for the narrative judges will remember. | If purely real data is chosen, the demo is unimpeachable but the modernisation story weakens, because the real corpora are PHP and TypeScript. If purely synthetic, the numbers are unfalsifiable and a sceptical judge will say so. |
| Q5 | Real GitHub merge gate vs local CLI | **Real gate, staged.** Local pipeline first, bob\_sessions/ committed early, GitHub Action wired only once the core works. | If time collapses, drop the Action and ship the local CLI with an exit-code gate. Never let the mandatory artefact be the thing that is broken at hour 22\. |
| Q6 | Headline claim | **Spec-mutation detection rate.** The review-debt delta is the “so what”, not the headline. | A time-saved claim is easier to say in 90 seconds but is crowded, unverifiable, and every competitor makes it. The spec-mutation number is novel, reproducible, and falsifiable — which is why it is worth the extra sentence of explanation. |

**B.1   Settled decisions**

| \# | Question | Decision | Rationale |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Q1 | Solo or team? | **Team of five** | Five critical paths, five sets of mandatory Bob evidence, one shared 40-Bobcoin pool. Allocation in §6.1. Contingency: reducing to three roughly doubles Bobcoins per person. |
| Q2 | Hackathon entry or company seed? | **Venture, with a hackathon-shaped demo** | The demo is a real, publishable measurement rather than a stunt, so the two objectives do not conflict. Building the pipeline honestly makes the demo fall out of it. |
| Q3 | Which vertical? | **IBM Z / legacy modernisation, adjacent to regulated** | Highest-budget pain in IBM's own catalogue, weakest incumbent tooling, and a vertical corpus is defensible in a way horizontal intent verification never is. The cost — no real mainframe in the room — is handled by simulating a realistic estate locally and saying so plainly. |

**B.2   A note on sources**

| A WARNING ABOUT THE CITATION LANDSCAPE A large fraction of the searchable “mainframe modernisation statistics” space is AI-generated content recycling invented numbers with real-sounding attribution, and those statistics keep being rediscovered and re-cited. The two worst examples are the “1.5 trillion lines of COBOL” figure and the “9 months with 14 engineers → 3 days” Blue Pearl case study, which exists in three versions differing by two orders of magnitude of effort — and which IBM's own case study describes as roughly 30 days and a 30+ person-day effort reduced to 3 days with a 2-person team, on a Java 11→25 uplift rather than a COBOL re-platform. Everything in this document was traced to a primary source, a dated analyst publication, or an explicitly labelled assumption. Where a number could not be verified, it was left out and listed in §A.5 rather than included for texture. |
